newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Aga Khan criticises press coverage of Islam.
newsitem.headline: Aga Khan criticises press coverage of Islam.

text.p: The Aga Khan, spiritual leader of 15 million Ismaili Moslems, on Thursday castigated "superficial and misleading" world press coverage of Islam.

In a wide-ranging address to the Commonwealth Press Union in Cape Town, the Aga Khan, himself a publisher, called for better educated journalists, a curb on the media profit motive and a better balance between press freedom and press responsibility.
"As an example of the need for greater expertise...I refer to the superficial and misleading way in which much of the world's media treats the world of Islam.
"The cultural contexts in which over one billion Moslems have been reared and shaped are simply not understood in much of the world," he said.
The Aga Khan criticised coverage of Islamic justice, saying reports of extremist actions did not necessarily represent the majority of the Islamic world.

Answering questions later, he said Islam's treatment of women, who are often denied any role outside the home, was not a deliberate policy of marginalisation. "The essence is to protect women from improper societal behaviour."
In his speech, he said few journalists were able to provide a context for events in Islamic societies.
"There is even a tendency to see political violence as a function of the faith itself, when in fact nothing could be further from the truth," he said.
The Aga Khan, founder and publisher of the East African Nation Printers and Publishers, said the world's media owners faced three crucial challenges.
"It is no longer enough that a journalist be a curious layman... Good journalists in our time must be well educated journalists," he said.
The second challenge was to move away from profit as the sole motive for publishing, he said, adding: "The runaway profit motive is a culprit that must be curbed."
The third challenge, he said, would be to ensure responsible journalism in a world of "obsessive individualism".
"In my view, we are sometimes too preoccupied with the rights of the press to be an independent social critic.
"The problem comes when freedom of the press is...used to shield the press, not just from government interference, but from any sense of social accountability," he said.
